transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hello, doctor. Thank you. Well, it’s... it’s a bit hard to pin down exactly when it started, but I suppose what finally got me here, sitting in this chair, is that my concentration has just gotten completely unreliable. And I mean, I'm a dentist, I've been practicing for decades, so focus is entirely necessary for my day-to-day. You can't exactly be distracted with a drill in your hand, right? 

But lately, I’ll be sitting at the clinic, just trying to review a patient's chart before I go in for a procedure, and... well, or even when I'm at home, actually. I paint—watercolors mostly, it's supposed to be how I unwind after looking at teeth all week—but I'll be laying out a watercolor wash on the paper, and suddenly I realize I've just been staring into space. I'll have read the same line in that patient chart three times over, or my brush will just be hovering there drying out, because my mind has completely wandered off. And it’s not wandering to, you know, pleasant daydreams or what I'm having for dinner. It just drifts to everything that could possibly go wrong. Every little worst-case scenario just spirals in my head. It's like I just can't keep my mind tethered to the actual task in front of me anymore, and frankly, it's really starting to bother me.
Doctor: Can you tell me if you find yourself worrying excessively about different things in your life, beyond just work or painting—like everyday situations, health, or responsibilities?

Well, yes, actually. It’s funny you phrase it that way, because it really does feel like my mind just keeps circling and circling around all sorts of things, and it’s rarely just one thing, you know? Like, take the practice, for instance. I've been slowly transitioning out, trying to hand things over to the younger associates, which you’d think would be a relief. But instead, I’m constantly fretting about whether my old patients—people I’ve treated for twenty, thirty years—are really being looked after properly. I mean, I know the new dentists are capable, they went to good schools, but my mind just latches onto this idea that they might miss something I would have caught. 

And then it’s not just the patients. I start worrying about the financial side of the handoff. Is the buyout structured right? What if the market dips and the practice valuation tanks right before I officially step away? I’ll spend hours running numbers in my head while I’m trying to fall asleep. And then, of course, that spirals into this whole other existential dread about retirement itself. I mean, what am I going to do with myself? Will I just become completely useless once I’m fully retired? I've been "Dr. Miller" for so long, if I'm not fixing teeth, who am I? Just an old man ruining watercolor paper? 

It’s exhausting. And the frustrating part is, a part of me knows it’s ridiculous. I know the worry feels completely out of proportion even to me. I mean, I’ve planned for retirement for decades, the practice is financially solid, my patients will be fine. But knowing that doesn't stop the thoughts from just spinning like a top. It’s like I can’t turn off the alarm bells in my head, even when there's no fire. It just bleeds into everything—everyday situations, responsibilities, you name it. It's just a constant, low-level hum of dread about what's coming next.
Have you noticed any physical symptoms, like feeling restless, being easily fatigued, or having tense muscles, especially when you're worrying?

Physical symptoms... well, it's interesting you bring up fatigue, because that is exactly what's been bothering me most on that front. I used to be the kind of guy who could work a ten-hour day at the clinic, doing complex root canals and crown preps, and still come home with plenty of gas in the tank. But lately? It’s like someone just pulls the plug on me. 

By midafternoon, I hit this absolute wall and I feel completely worn out. And it’s not just being a little sleepy, you know? It's a deep, dragging sort of exhaustion. The really frustrating part is that resting doesn't even touch it. I'll try to take it easy on my days off, thinking maybe a quiet morning with the newspaper or a quick nap on the couch will reset my battery, but it doesn't fix it at all. I wake up feeling just as drained as before I closed my eyes, probably because my mind hasn't actually rested, it's just been churning through all those worries we just talked about. 

Because of this, even the simplest things are starting to feel like monumental chores. Like weeding the garden—we have these raised beds out back that I usually love tending to, but getting out there with the trowel just feels so much heavier than it used to. Or even standing at my easel for my watercolors. Just standing there, trying to paint, my arms and legs feel heavy. It's almost like I'm wearing one of those lead aprons we put on patients for dental X-rays, just carrying that weight around all day. So yes, the fatigue is very real, and it just makes everything I try to do feel like I'm wading through wet cement.
Have you been having trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking up too early in the morning?

Sleep? Oh, sleep has become an absolute nightmare, if you'll pardon the pun. It’s just... it’s so frustrating because, like I said, I’m exhausted. I’m physically dragging by the end of the day. So, most nights, I get into bed, and I’m genuinely tired. My eyes are heavy, my body aches from standing at the chair or just from carrying that invisible lead apron around all day. I pull up the covers, turn off the lamp, and I think, "Finally, I can just shut down." 

But the second—and I mean the absolute second—the house gets quiet, it’s like someone flips a switch in my brain. My wife, Susan, she falls asleep the moment her head hits the pillow. I can hear her breathing slow down, and I’m just lying there in the dark, staring at the ceiling fan. And that’s when it starts. The reel starts playing. I start replaying every single patient transfer I did that week. Did I tell Dr. Evans about Mrs. Gable’s sensitivity on tooth number 14? Did he write it down? And then from there, it jumps straight to the money details. I’ll be lying there at midnight, literally doing compound interest math in my head, worrying about the practice valuation, wondering if I should have negotiated a different payout structure. 

It takes me hours to finally drift off. And then, even when I do finally manage to fall asleep, it’s not good sleep. It’s thin. It’s fragile. I’m tossing, I’m turning, and inevitably, my eyes snap open at four or five in the morning. And I’m wide awake. Not refreshed awake, mind you, but that anxious, heart-pounding kind of awake. I’ll look at the clock—4:12 AM—and I know it’s over. I’m not going back to sleep. I just lie there feeling like I never really settled down in the first place, like my brain was just idling in a high gear all night. So I just get up and wander around the house, maybe make a pot of coffee I don't even want, just waiting for the sun to come up. It's a terrible way to start the day, every single day.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy, like painting or tending to your garden?

Well, no, not exactly lost interest. I mean, it's not that I don't care about the garden or the watercolors anymore. I still want to do them. It's just... well, like I was saying before about the fatigue, it's more about the energy it takes to do them now. 

Take the watercolors, for instance. I've always loved the process, you know? Setting up the easel by the window in the sunroom, getting the lighting just right, mixing the pigments... I used to get lost in it for hours on a Sunday afternoon. I still look at my brushes and think, "I should really work on that landscape of the coast I started last month." The desire is there. But when I actually go to do it, I just feel so drained. I'll stand there, and my arms feel heavy, and my mind is just too clouded with all those other worries we talked about. I can't seem to find that quiet space in my head that I used to need to really focus on the colors and the brushstrokes. 

And it's the same with the garden. I still love seeing the tomatoes come in, and I still want the beds to look nice. I haven't suddenly decided I hate gardening. It's just that getting out there, kneeling in the dirt, pulling the weeds... it feels like such a monumental effort now. I'll look out the kitchen window at the raised beds and think, "I really need to get out there and thin those seedlings," but I just don't have the stamina. I end up just sitting in the kitchen, feeling guilty about not doing it, while simultaneously worrying about everything else. So, the interest is still there, definitely. It's just... the enjoyment is being smothered by how exhausted and preoccupied I am all the time.
Would you say you feel down or depressed most of the time, even when there’s nothing specific to worry about?

Down or depressed? No... no, I wouldn't say that. It's really not a sadness, if that makes sense. I mean, I know what depression looks like—my sister went through a terrible bout of it after her divorce years ago, where she just couldn't see the point of anything and cried all the time. That's not me. I don't feel hopeless, and I don't feel like crying. I don't walk around with a dark cloud of sadness over my head. 

It's really just the worrying. It's the constant, unyielding tension of the worry that grinds me down. If I could just turn off the thoughts about the practice transition, the finances, the "what ifs," I think I'd be perfectly happy. Like, if Susan and I were sitting on the porch and my brain was actually quiet for once, I'd feel fine. I'd feel like my old self. But because my brain is always running that ticker tape of concerns, I end up feeling exhausted and overwhelmed. So, if I look unhappy, it's not because I'm depressed or feeling down about life in general. It's just that I'm so incredibly tired of being on high alert all the time. I'm just worn out from the anxiety of it all, not depressed.
